`as const` freezes a value to its narrowest literal type (readonly, literal strings/tuples) but doesn't check it against anything. `satisfies` checks the value against a type without widening it, so you keep the precise inferred type and still get errors for typos. They combine well: `const routes = { home: '/' } as const satisfies Record<string, string>`. Action: none needed; point me at a spot in the repo if you want me to check which one fits.

There's a real difference, not just style. structuredClone keeps Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays and undefined values and handles circular references; the JSON round trip turns Dates into strings, Maps and Sets into {}, drops undefined and functions, and throws on cycles. structuredClone also throws on functions and loses class prototypes, so neither is a magic deep copy. Action: none; use structuredClone unless you specifically want JSON semantics.

A Deployment treats pods as interchangeable: any pod can be killed and replaced, names are random, and storage is shared or absent. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable name (like db-0, db-1), stable DNS, ordered start and stop, and its own persistent volume that follows it. Pick the StatefulSet when instances need identity or their own disk, such as databases, Kafka or other clustered stores. Action: none needed; tell me if you want this applied to a specific service of ours.

tsx compiles each file with esbuild and just strips types, so it starts almost instantly and handles ESM, CJS and tsconfig paths with no config, but it never type-checks. ts-node uses the real TypeScript compiler, so it type-checks at run time but is slower and ESM needs more setup. Use tsx for running scripts and keep `tsc --noEmit` in CI. Action: none for the question; just remember the lockfile isn't updated yet after the package.json edit.
